query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a machine‐learning–augmented multiscale simulation framework that explicitly incorporates hierarchical microstructural descriptors (e.g., local phase fractions, nanoprecipitate distributions, and grain boundary configurations) will allow faster (and more accurate) predictions of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior in HfNbTiVAl10 than conventional full-scale DFT/finite-element simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure characterized by distinct nano‐to‐microscale morphological features.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a predictive framework that uses descriptors derived from both atomic-scale (e.g., DFT-calculated pairwise interaction features) and microscale (e.g., image‐based microstructural segmentation) information, training machine learning models to map these descriptors to mechanical properties under tensile and fracture loading.
generation.conditions: Tensile and fracture testing under controlled strain rates and temperatures similar to those used in experimental validation of HfNbTiVAl10; the model is developed using a training dataset compiled from related refractory and high-entropy alloy studies.
generation.structural_mediator: The hierarchical heterostructure (including variations in local modulus from nanoprecipitates, grain boundaries, and phase interfaces) acts as the mediator between the atomic-level descriptors and the macroscopic mechanical response.
generation.mechanism: By combining atomic-level interaction insights (as demonstrated in ML predictions for refractory alloys) with spatially resolved microstructural descriptors, the model dynamically adjusts predictions of elastic and plastic deformation as well as fracture initiation, effectively capturing the influence of the hierarchical structure. This more focused, data-driven approach reduces the computational burden relative to full first-principles and finite-element simulations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The new framework is predicted to reduce simulation time by up to 50% and improve prediction accuracy (e.g., lowering error metrics by approximately 10–20%) for key mechanical properties (Young’s modulus, yield strength, and initial fracture behavior) compared with conventional simulation methods.
generation.baseline: Standard simulation approaches such as full DFT calculations combined with finite-element analyses, which are computationally intensive and have larger uncertainties in mapping complex heterostructured features to mechanical response.
generation.boundary: The approach may fail when the microstructural descriptors cannot capture critical non‐linear damage mechanisms (e.g., under extreme strain rates, very high temperature, or if the heterogeneity is not adequately resolved by available imaging techniques). Additionally, if the training dataset lacks sufficient diversity, the mapping from structure to property may be unreliable.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from analogous machine learning predictions in other refractory/high-entropy alloy systems supports the approach, the exact quantitative gains in efficiency and accuracy for HfNbTiVAl10 remain uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Develop the ML-augmented multiscale simulation framework for HfNbTiVAl10 and perform tensile and fracture tests to measure Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness. Compare the simulation predictions (in terms of both accuracy and computational time) to those obtained via established DFT/finite-element methods as well as direct experimental measurements.
measurements: Fracture toughness or related fracture parameters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-augmented framework does not reduce simulation time by at least 50% and fails to achieve a minimum 10% improvement in prediction accuracy (relative to established methods) or produces predictions that lie outside the error bounds of experimental results, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Atomic Interaction-Based Prediction of Phase Formations in High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are of particular interest due to their unique combination of high strength, ductility, and fracture resistance. These properties are largely impacted by the phases and number of phases present in the alloy. Due to the enormous chemical design space, with typically five or six elements present in the alloys in addition to the various processing parameters, the prediction of the number of phases is challenging. While there have been multiple recent reports of phase predictions through data-driven models, an alternate approach is proposed and demonstrated here. In this work, phase prediction is performed using features derived from DFT-calculated pairwise interactions among constituent elements (incorporating bonding and structure) rather than relying solely on traditional elemental descriptors such as electronegativity. By focusing on atomic interaction features, our model provides a novel perspective on the phase stability in HEAs. Predicting Elastic Constants of Refractory Complex Concentrated Alloys Using Machine Learning Approach

Abstract: AbstractRefractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) have drawn increasing attention recently owing to their balanced mechanical properties, including excellent creep resistance, ductility, and oxidation resistance. The mechanical and thermal properties of RCCAs are directly linked with the elastic constants. However, it is time consuming and expensive to obtain the elastic constants of RCCAs with conventional trial-and-error experiments. The elastic constants of RCCAs are predicted using a combination of density functional theory simulation data and machine learning (ML) algorithms in this study. The elastic constants of several RCCAs are predicted using the random forest regressor, gradient boosting regressor (GBR), and XGBoost regression models. Based on performance metrics R-squared, mean average error and root mean square error, the GBR model was found to be most promising in predicting the elastic constant of RCCAs among the three ML models.
